text: Most hybrid quantum-classical projects don't fail because the quantum circuit was wrong. They fail because of classical architecture decisions made in the first week. Here are five that recur constantly, so you can recognize them before they cost real money.

Developing straight against real hardware instead of a simulator. No retry or fallback for a flaky remote job. No cost ceiling on the optimization loop. Ignoring shot noise when comparing two results. And coupling your orchestration code tightly to one provider's SDK. Notice something: none of these five is the quantum circuit being logically wrong.

Here's mistake three's fix, built right into the console: Amazon Braket's real Spending limits page. A loop that fails to converge — oscillating, plateauing, diverging from a bug — can burn through a full iteration budget at real-hardware prices before anyone notices, unless cumulative spend is tracked and capped inside the loop itself, not just reviewed after the fact on a billing dashboard.

And here's mistake two's territory: a real quantum task detail page, showing status, shot count, and where results land. Cloud quantum providers have queues, recalibration windows, and transient failures like any remote service. A hybrid loop with no retry logic will crash or silently return bad data the first time a submission times out — and in production, that's a real incident, not a demo hiccup.

Mistake four, made visible: this is a real measured noise-decay plot from IBM Quantum's own hardware. A measured value's standard error shrinks only as the square root of shot count — at a thousand shots, that's already around three percent. Two results that differ by less than that aren't evidence of a real difference. They're noise, and treating noise as signal leads to wrong conclusions about which design is actually better.

Every one of these five mistakes is something a backend engineer would recognize instantly in a non-quantum microservice. That's the whole point of this course — the quantum-specific knowledge is a small, learnable slice; the production discipline around it is the discipline you already know. Chapter 2 moves into the classical sandwich around every circuit, starting with getting your data in correctly.
